sourceText: cells: Mr, Mx, Mo Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the SANDERSON-INVESTITURE-LAB sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. Kesh treats magic as a conserved resource and finds an exploit that removes a cost believed to be fundamental. The memorial bore the name of Brandon Sanderson precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Vela observed that many magical systems were more explicit about cost than technologies were: the price was sometimes written into ontology rather than hidden in a supply chain. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. Darin was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Darin had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Darin, the speculative mechanism was not an 313 ‘idea.’ It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: Publishing the discovery could democratize power or collapse institutions built around the old price. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Mr — Resource Magic: power is stored in resources; Mx — Exchange Magic: every intervention exacts a cost; Mo — Ontological Oath: breaking a promise produces consequences. Course references included Brandon Sanderson; exchange magic; oath fantasy. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Tern broke the first consensus. ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ Vela answered without raising their voice: ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not lack entertainment. She lacked the resistance of things to the model. 314 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS When she could anticipate every reaction, the world became functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. Kesh leaves without a verdict and understands that technical understanding does not automatically confer a mandate to optimize. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. The outside residue had become stable enough that Tern could predict where it would not appear: in sectors fully indexed by Aster. He began to believe that the message carried no content at all, but instead demonstrated a boundary — a region in which their instruments received no echo from their own creator. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the BOUNDARY operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — moves, perforates, or redefines the boundary between inside and outside — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a 315 copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 316 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
